subject: Preserve Abravanel Hall
comment: Hello, City Council! • My name is Rosalie Lund Macmillan. I am a lifelong Utahn. My family has lived in Utah for generations. • I come from a very musical and artistic family, which is not uncommon in Utah. The arts are deeply embedded in our Utah culture and have been for generations. • The National Endowment for the Arts ranks Utah number one in the nation for live participation in the arts. • I believe the greatest catalyst for the explosive growth of the arts in Utah was the creation of Abravanel Hall. • Our relatively small community voted to raise the funds and many donated very generously so that we could build a world-class concert hall. What does that say about our community and our priorities in Utah? • It was the greatest hall in the West. People traveled from all over the country to come. It was designed by the acoustic genius who designed the famous Avery Fisher Hall in New York. I've been told it's one of the top three acoustical halls on the planet. • When you have a world-class hall, you are able to host world-class music. My family got to meet Yo-Yo Ma and help him name his cello. I got to meet Itzhak Perlman. I got to hear Jessye Norman sing in person. I had the opportunity to be mentored by the great Joseph Silverstein. Would any of this have happened if we didn't have Abravanel Hall? Absolutely not! This world-class hall attracted world-class talent which then brought even more talent and extraordinary teachers into our community. The existence of Abravanel Hall has directly affected the trajectory of my life and the lives of many others. • We didn't have to fly to New York City or the great capitals of Europe in order to be exposed to the world's greatest music and musicians. Incredibly, we got to experience that right here in our relatively much smaller hometown. • Abravanel Hall was brand new when I was a little girl. It was called Symphony Hall back then. I attended regularly with my family then, and have attended ever since. Now I attend with my young children. • Many of the strongest core memories of my life have taken place in Abravanel Hall. • I still remember the moment vividly when I was about seven years old, staring up at the beautiful chandeliers, and feeling overwhelmed by the gorgeous music I was hearing when I made the conscious decision that I wanted to be a musician when I grew up. I decided right then and there that my lifelong goal was going to be to play on that glorious stage one day. • I assure you I was not the only kid who has had that dream. There is a whole generation of us who grew up listening to world-class music in Abravanel Hall. There are hundreds of us from that first Youth Guild that was formed, so many of us checking costs in order to get extra tickets. I have kept in touch with many of them over the years. We have grown up to become music lovers, both amateurs and professionals, some nominated for Grammys, others breaking records on YouTube, and even some who play in the hall every week as members of our Utah Symphony. Collectively, our music students number in the tens of thousands. We are in turn influencing a new generation of music lovers who also have access to world-class music because of our world-class hall. • My most recent core memory in Abravanel Hall took place at one of the many concerts I have attended with my children. I looked over to see my young daughter, completely lost in the music, and gazing up at the chandeliers like I used to as a child. My young son leaned in and whispered, "Do you think I could do that someday?" motioning to the musicians onstage. I whispered back, "Absolutely." • I'd like to see my kids on that stage. I'd like to see my grandkids on that stage! • Our community made waves when they first built this hall and sent a really strong message about the priority of arts in our community. What message are you sending to our arts-loving community if you destroy it? Thank you for your consideration. Rosalie Macmillan

subject: SECC Participation Agreement - Japantown
comment: Hello City Council, I unfortunately ran out of time and wanted to share my full comments on the Participation Agreement: Mayor Mendenhall, City Council Members and staff, Thank you for your time. My name is Marisa Eng and I am a member of the SLC NextGen JA group and Salt Lake Buddhist Temple Board. I wanted to speak today in regards to the participation agreement that was voted on earlier this evening. First, I want to thank each of you, as well as our community leaders, SEG and the public for listening and for your advocacy and commitment to preserving and revitalizing Japantown. It was very heartening to see Japantown included in the participation agreement with the $5million earmarked for revitalization efforts and for working to include us in the planning and development conversations to come. It feels like a step in the right direction. While it is a positive step forward and probably felt like somewhat of a sprint, I know this process will be a marathon and there is still a long road ahead to work out the details. After reading through the agreement, I want to acknowledge that I am still cautious and there are still several concerns that I want to ensure are considered as the process continues with you, SEG, the County, and State. As longtime neighbors and community stakeholders, it is crucial that the Salt Lake Buddhist Temple and Japanese Church of Christ are involved in the process and we welcome and encourage discussions more than twice a year as well as having ongoing dialogue and partnership post development. I also want to ensure that we preserve the temple, church and garden that is there today. The daily and annual festival operations should be able to continue without disruption from additional traffic and throughout construction. I ask that we continue to work with the county and state on parking arrangements for festivals and road accessibility for daily function and festivals. Lastly, I am hopeful that we can meaningfully honor the work and legacy of our Japanese American ancestors. Let's continue what was started with the RDA streetscape to reimagine and develop Japantown to be a space that welcomes and celebrates the diversity, culture, and history of Japantown. Along with the streetscape, having Japanese or minority-owned small businesses or spaces on the street can help cultivate that vision and activate a cultural and economic hub for all to enjoy. Thank you. Marisa Eng

comment: Dear SLC Council, I find it very disheartening that sports are yet again taking precedence over the arts. I've spent my whole life learning and enjoying music and watching sports get all the recognition and funding and it's discouraging. Is what you hear at a game different than what the Utah Symphony plays? Absolutely. Does that make either genre any less valuable? No. Music influences everyone daily, whether they realize it or not. If it were absent everyone would notice that there's something amazing missing from the world. Does the building need updates? Yes. I would think those would be cheaper to do than a whole new building. But if the plan is ready to build a new one it needs to be planned and completed completed before the hall is demolished. Taking away the beautiful hall where one of only 15 full time professional orchestras plays without having a better hall in place would be a disservice to the community and to all the people whose livelihoods depend on having somewhere to create and work. I have played at the hall multtismed and there is nowhere else I've played in this state that even comes close to the experience, either as a performer or a listener. The Symphony is one of the only reasons I even venture downtown and spend my money on dinner there or in the mall as I wander through on the way to a concert. I'm sure there are many others that feel the same. I believe removing the venue would be more of detriment to the downtown economy than you might expect. I believe sports and music can coexist and bring value to the community as they are already doing, but music's influence and growth should not be stunted by the loss of such a beautiful space. I hope you will come to the same conclusion. Thanks, Kirstin Hoyt

subject: CIP Funding for the Liberty Park Greenhouse (Liberty Park Greenhouse - Envisioned / D5
comment: The Greenhouse at Liberty Park was built before 1922. It was beautiful! I remember being inside it many times over the years, and it was very depressing to see it fall into disrepair. Why do we do that in Salt Lake City? This building has an incredible amount of opportunity to educate our younger generations of students, right next to where they play. Make growing plants fun. I know it is a lot of fun for me. We are on the cusp of an ecological disaster where our planet is going to implode, and it will be too late. There is such an opportunity to teach the children of Salt Lake City about climate and how the right plants can make a huge difference. We should use the greenhouse to fill this void. Think of the educational classes you can have in the greenhouse, as well as outside in some or all of the open spaces that are around the greenhouse. Perhaps you show comparisons, building a normal Salt Lake garden of flowers, and track the water use to keep them alive. On the other side of the field, grow a garden that uses much less water, but looks just as pretty. Show the various waterwise grasses that will grow easily in Utah. This could be an educational piece of the Youth City program, teaching how to grow plants from seed, and then move them out into the open air and eventually harvest the tomatoes and other vegetables. It could be a wonderful field trip for elementary children around the valley. On Saturdays you could have demonstration classes outside that would include parents and children. There are so many educators here that could be the teachers, perhaps eventually teaching the Parks staff how to teach about plants and what makes them grow. It is also a great opportunity to teach people about trees and how they do need water even though they have been growing for 15 years without any water. Wait until the next windstorm, when the trees fall over because they aren't getting the water they need. Ask the Forestry Department and the Cemetery folks, what it takes to grow a tree. Show them a hollow, unwatered tree give the people of Utah the knowledge they need to keep the vegetation on earth alive, for their children. One class in second grade won't do it. It needs to be built into everyday life. Use the greenhouse and the space around it to start, and continue, that conversation. Fixing the greenhouse so it is usable is a small price to pay. Please approve the CIP funding for the restoration of this greenhouse. Judi Short

subject: Manufactured Housing in Allen Park
comment: Hello Dan, Late last summer or early fall by chance I met with Palmer DePaulis at an Allen Park special open house. They were holding a special event to let the public, especially their supporters, know about future for the complex. There were several options including different new buildings for several different proposed uses. Any and all of it seemed feasible. I haven't heard one thing about it since. In the meantime here at Crossroads we have been collaborating with one of our long time volunteers, Jeff White, on the possibility of providing manufactured housing for lower income residents of the city. I fact Jeff is under contract with the city housing authority to consult with them on various lower cost housing options. What Jeff has documented is that truly decent, affordable housing can be made available to lower income residents. So what? Several things. First, as I recall the Allen Park proposed plans offered the probability that some of the housing units would be made available to lower income individuals and maybe even families. I believe the intent is the units would house younger specialists with a particular interest in Allen Park, its history and environmental surrounding. Second, Jeff's special knowledge of the lower income housing and, especially, manufactured housing marks it as a feasible housing alternative in Allen Park. Palmer DePaulis sits on the city housing authority board and as a former mayor and public figure has shown a continuing concern for lower income residents. Palmer needs to know about manufactured housing and the city housing authority's interest. Third, Jeff, as a contractor cannot contact Palmer on his own. He feels it would be unprofessional for him to do so. I could try talking to Palmer but that might not get things going like it should. Help is needed. Upon a request from me representing Crossroads Urban Center would you be willing to listen to Jeff's manufactured housing proposal? If you find it promising would you contact Palmer and tell him as much. Then Palmer in turn can ask the housing authority staff what the situation might be. It could be the right thing for Allen Park and for some the other low income housing opportunities in the city. Plus you get a bird's eye view of the situation. Is this over reaching? No, not really. Manufactured housing is a real, ready to go option. The city housing authority can help deliver it in fast order. Like six months or so. Including Allen Park there are several building sites in on city owned property ready to go. Finally, just to be clear. I am doing this as a community advocate for the sake of the potential homeowners. Jeff is on a humble contract and just wants to get things moving. If it makes any difference to you we are also Judge Memorial graduates. Years apart we are but here to help out all the same. Thank you, Tim Funk Crossroads Urban Center

subject: Taxpayers don't want to subsidize stadium
comment: Dear City Councilmember: I urge you to oppose the proposed citywide sales tax increase that would give nearly $1 billion to the NHL sports/entertainment district. Inflation and growth have substantially increased the cost of housing, food, energy and other essential household expenses in recent years. These compounding costs amount to more than $11,000 a year for the average family of four! Many Salt Lake City residents simply cannot afford the additional estimated cost of $225 per year if this sales tax increase is approved. comment: Hi All, We now have about 180 completed surveys. Again, all are campers in SLC and all are struggling with a mental health or addiction problem. I was in Burger King on 400S 600W last night for about a half hour and counted what appeared to be 8 campers entering or leaving. I now understand I can just sit at any trax stop or corner in the downtown area and collect 20 surveys in about four hours. I can sit there reading a book, relaxing and get 20 surveys completed in no time. Easy. 6 days / 20 surveys will give us the 300 we need as a base for creating what could be a new narrative. Or we can visit any of the camps in the area and get a real glimpse of a "what it's like to be mentally ill and addicted in Salt Lake City" experience. We may not have been asking enough questions on the number, types and names of the programs all these folks living on our streets have been in. The average arrests is 20. We have an extra chair if anyone would like to join us. Bernie

subject: Efficacy
comment: Hi All, The following was sent to a person interested in our effort to create an awareness of the current mental health "we can help you" systems level of effectiveness as it relates to homelessness and suicide. 3. I have been surveying the homeless campers in the area. 180 surveys. 80% of those I approached did the survey. 100% are dealing with a mental health or addiction problem. 100% have been in a "we can help you" program. A small follow up sample survey showed they had been arrested on average 20x and have been in at least 12 programs. That's 32 opportunities the current system had to help them and it failed. .....so all, is what we are doing actually helping people dealing with mental health and addictions issues? subject: SEG Project - Revitalization Tax
comment: Good Day All! You may have noted that many Salt Lake residents have expressed concern over the Rev Tax on citizens, especially that the tax will not be shared outright with surrounding communities. For me, as a community leader with the North West Community Council, the concern is particularly applicable as our west side communities are populated by lower income statuses than other parts of the city. Considerations to share revenue in your deliberations: 1. Lower the tax rate; 2. appropriate 10% of the current tax rate with residents, forming an advisory committee noting how such a share will be spent perhaps in the form of Item 3; and, 3. Create an interlocal agreement such as exists with the Utah Inland Port Authority whereby revenue is shared with the community: "The Parties desire to enter into this Agreement to comply with Utah law, to establish a contractual relationship creating certainty on the 25-year distribution of the City Differential to UIPA and to commit to a process for the expenditure of a portion of the City Differential". For many, the tax issue condenses to fairness: A) city residents paying for a statewide public benefit, B) the burden on financially vulnerable communities, C) increased traffic/infrastructure burden on the city from statewide and national attendees, and, D) communities have had limited time to review the recently released contract. For example, before reaching a decision, hold public meetings to gain input; some may be negative but others may offer insights on how to improve the tax issue. Public outreach will also improve public trust. Best, Terry Marasco

subject: traffic calming on Ken Rey St
comment: Dear Jon and Dan, First of all, thank you for your consistent efforts to improve pedestrian safety in Salt Lake City. It is comforting to know that we share the vision of a city where pedestrians and cyclists have an equal right to safe passage on streets as motorists. Re-training drivers to be courteous and careful is a tall order and the Bonneville Road Safety Committee appreciates your support and funding for traffic calming. The measures being implemented are saving lives. A member of our committee, Eddie Karasik, brought to our attention this week that the City was able to install traffic calming white pylons where Kensington Ave, Bryan Ave, and Ken Rey St merge. Given the width of Ken Rey and the lack of signage approaching this intersection, speeding and disorder have been the norm. If three roads meet and no drivers are instructed to yield, at some point a bad accident is bound to occur where two drivers assume they have the right of way or try to beat the other car through the intersection. Eddie mentioned that the white pylons seem to be doing a good job of slowing drivers and directing them around the middle of the intersection rather than right through it. However, some neighbors do not like how the white pylons look and it sounds like they have been voicing their concerns. I wonder if the City and this neighborhood could come together and meet both safety needs and aesthetic preferences by installing a small roundabout in this intersection. I happen to live just below where Princeton Ave, Herbert Ave, and Yale Ave meet and the small (greenery-filled) roundabout is attractive and helps all cars navigate this intersection safely. I have attached both a picture of the roundabout as well as a map. Please let me know how we, as a committee and concerned neighborhood citizens, can support the City's efforts to fulfill the Livable Streets Program's traffic calming improvements on Ken Rey St. Looking forward to hearing your thoughts, Lauren

subject: My thoughts on the sports complex
comment: Dan, I'm not sure what happened and why you voted in favor of this. I think you owe it to D6 to be transparent about these things before voting and the lack of transparency is really troubling. Here's the reality, from the mouths of experts: "These are luxury palaces that are being built that are exclusive and limited to some of the wealthiest people in the city," Bradbury said. "So why is the government subsidizing this? These could easily be privately funded and we know that because that's how baseball came into existence." "There's no evidence that stadiums are economic development catalysts and, in fact, they tend to have some very big detriments," he said, noting that they bring crime and their sporadic use can discourage stable businesses like grocery stores. "They're just very bad anchors for economic development," Bradbury said. "This bill is a lose-lose for Utah taxpayers, who will face higher taxes and fewer public services as a result," said AFP-Utah executive director Kevin Greene. "While every Utahn would be excited for new sports teams, the wealthy sports franchises who want new stadiums should foot the bill themselves. If a billion dollars of hardworking families' money is the price to play ball, Utah shouldn't play the game at all." It's clear that SLC residents should not be footing the bill. We deserve an explanation for why you voted how you did. Brad. On Tue, Jul 9, 2024 at 6:58 PM Brad Bush <[redacted-email]> wrote: Dan, Just reiterating my opposition to the use of taxpayer funds to support the SEG stadium work. This entire initiative is very focused on glossy pictures and light on details and a project with all the telltale signs of a major money loser for residents to the benefit of a multi-billionaire. The only fathomable rationale for this would be that the city could guarantee higher benefit than cost to each resident. Otherwise, this just becomes a wealth transfer tax hike. But all the economic analysis on this topic points to these kinds of boondoggles as money losers for residents. The primary driver for people like Mendenhall is to burnish image, which is a benefit pocketed in real time, while the community pays costs over decades. Key institutions like Abravanel Hall shouldn't be impacted. Ultimately, Smith has few options besides SLC and he loses going south. If there's a path for the city to benefit without financial contribution, tax hikes or negative impact to existing institutions, great. But none of us should be footing the bill or paying the price for this. SLC would be better off passing on this than having this project blight the downtown and putting residents on the hook for the bill. And I'll also be candid that the lack of communication from your side on walking on this issue and the details on what's on the table needs to be better. A D6 newsletter would do a lot to keep residents updated. Brad
